name: Oblique shock
seoDesc: Oblique shock: work out a term from the pressure and the stagnation pressure. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Oblique shock calculator turns the pressure, the stagnation pressure and more into a term. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Oblique shock calculator work?
sections.html:
The Oblique shock calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports a term in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the pressure (p₁), the stagnation pressure (p₀₁), the temperature (T₂) (Upstream) and the wave angle (β).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Oblique shock calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

A term=(mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) ^ 2) × (the sine of (wave angle (β)), 2)
A term=tnum1 + 1
Specific heat ratio (γ)=(-(mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) ^ 2) × the cosine of (2 × wave angle (β)) + Tden 1 − 2) ÷ (mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) ^ 2)
Turn angle (θ)=(2 × Tnum 1 × (wave angle (β)) ÷ Tden 1)
A term=(mach number (Mₓ) (normal shock) ^ 2)
A term=(-M 2num − 4 × Tnum 1) ÷ (4 × specific heat ratio (γ) × Tnum 1 − (mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) ^ 2) × (specific heat ratio (γ) + 1 ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Specific heat ratio (γ) = 1.4, Mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) = 10 and Wave angle (β) = 10 deg. The calculator returns Mach number (Mₓ) (normal shock) = 1.7365, Turn angle (θ) = 5.5332 deg, Pressure ratio (p₂/p₁) = 3.3513 and Stagnation pressure ratio (p₀₂/p₀₁) = 0.8404.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mach number (Mₓ) (normal shock) = 1.7365, Turn angle (θ) = 5.5332 deg, Pressure ratio (p₂/p₁) = 3.3513 and Stagnation pressure ratio (p₀₂/p₀₁) = 0.8404 should be roughly the size you expected from Specific heat ratio (γ) = 1.4 and Mach number (M₁) (oblique shock) = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Pressure, opening in bars

  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Angle, opening in degrees

  • Pressure, opening in bars

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Oblique shock calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the pressure, the stagnation pressure and the temperature (T₂) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Oblique shock calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns a term, derived from the pressure, the stagnation pressure and the temperature (T₂). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Oblique shock calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pressure, the stagnation pressure, the temperature (T₂) and the wave angle, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pressure (p₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pressure (p₁) opens in bars and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mach number (Mₓ) (normal shock) = 1.7365. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Oblique shock calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
